title: Shaytan never asks for the whole thing. Only a step.
subtitle: Footsteps, and the grace that purifies

row.title: Allah purifies
sub: without Him, not one of us

then: Coming right after the slander, this verse names how it spread: {trap}step by step.{/trap} Qatadah said every sin is one of Shaytan's footsteps. Ibn Kathir explains that without Allah's grace {reward}no one would ever be purified,{/reward} since He is the one who helps people turn back.
now: It never starts with the scandal. It starts with opening the app "just to check." Then one comment. Then one reply you would not say to their face. {trap}Each step feels small.{/trap} The verse asks you to notice the first one, and to ask Allah for the purity you cannot make alone.
old: I would never do something that bad.
new: Big wrongs are small steps added up, and only Allah's grace keeps me pure.
try: Name one small first step that usually leads you somewhere you regret. Skip it once today.

title: Would you not love Allah to forgive you?
subtitle: Abu Bakr, Mistah, and the oath he took back

row.title: an oath
sub: I will never spend on him

then: Mistah was Abu Bakr's poor cousin, an emigrant who lived on what Abu Bakr spent on him. After Mistah joined the slander against Aishah, Abu Bakr swore never to help him again. When this verse came, he said, {reward}of course we love that You forgive us,{/reward} and {idea}resumed his spending forever.{/idea}
now: Your brother said something unforgivable about your spouse at a wedding. You cut him off. Now he is short on rent and calls you. This verse does not erase what he did. It asks you a question: {reward}would you not love Allah to forgive you?{/reward}
old: After what they did, I owe them nothing.
new: When I pardon those who wronged me, I am asking Allah to pardon me.
try: Think of one relative you have closed a door on. Send them one kind word, or one small help.

title: Slandering the innocent and unaware is a grave sin.
subtitle: Women who never even thought of what they were accused of
then: Ibn Kathir notes this was revealed because of Aishah, and the Mothers of the believers are first in it. He cites the hadith listing seven destructive sins, among them {trap}accusing chaste, unaware believing women.{/trap} Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd said it applies {idea}to anyone who does the same to Muslim women.{/idea}
now: She is the quiet girl at university. Someone invents a story about her and it spreads through three group chats. She has no idea. She just notices people staring. This verse stands with her. {idea}Her unawareness is part of her innocence,{/idea} and the weight falls on those talking.
old: If she did nothing, the gossip cannot really hurt her.
new: Allah counts slandering an innocent, unaware person among the most destructive sins.
try: If you know someone being talked about unfairly, quietly defend them once in the next conversation.

title: Your own tongue, hands and feet will testify.
subtitle: The witnesses you carry everywhere
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ described a servant who argues with his Lord, refusing any witness but himself. Allah says, {idea}you are enough as a witness against yourself.{/idea} His mouth is sealed and {trap}his limbs speak of his deeds.{/trap}
now: The thumb that typed it. The feet that walked into that room. The tongue that said "I swear I didn't." You carry your witnesses everywhere. {idea}They are listening now.{/idea} That is not a reason for fear alone. It is a reason to give them better things to say.
old: If I deny it well enough, it is as if it did not happen.
new: My own body keeps the record and will speak it plainly.
try: Tonight, look at your hands and ask: what did they do today that I would want them to tell?

title: That Day, everyone will see that Allah is the Truth.
subtitle: The account paid in full, with no unfairness
then: Ibn Abbas said the word here means {idea}their account.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains that on that Day people will know Allah's promise, His threat and His reckoning are {idea}all just, with no unfairness in them.{/idea}
now: The colleague who lied about you got promoted. The cousin who spread the story never apologized. It feels like they won. This verse is the long view: {idea}every account is paid in full.{/idea} You do not have to settle it yourself. You only have to make sure your own account is clean.
new: No one gets away with anything; the Truth settles every account in full.
try: Hand one unresolved wrong done to you over to Allah in a short dua, and stop replaying it today.

title: Evil words suit evil people. Aishah was free of them.
subtitle: What the slander says about those who spoke it
then: Ibn Abbas said this was revealed about Aishah and the people of the slander. Ibn Jarir explained that {trap}evil speech is more suited to evil people.{/trap} What the hypocrites said fit them, not her. Ibn Kathir adds it implies a promise that she will be {reward}the Prophet's ﷺ wife in Paradise.{/reward}
now: When someone tells you something ugly about another person, notice what it reveals. Often it says more about the speaker than the subject. {idea}Words carry the scent of where they come from.{/idea} And the words you choose about others say who you are.
old: When someone is accused of something ugly, it says something about them.
new: Ugly words usually describe the one who says them; good people are kept clear of them.
try: Listen to your own words about others for one day. Ask what they say about you.

title: A home is a private world. Knock and greet first.
subtitle: Asking permission puts people at ease

row.title: a formality
sub: we are close, just walk in

row.title: their ease
sub: Ibn Abbas: putting people at ease

then: Muqatil said that before Islam people walked straight into each other's homes, which was hard on those inside. Ibn Kathir reports that Jabir knocked and answered {trap}it is me{/trap} and the Prophet ﷺ disliked it. Abdullah bin Mas'ud would {idea}clear his throat at his own door{/idea} so his family was not startled.
now: Your teenager's bedroom. Your parents' room. A friend's flat where you have a key. A colleague's office door left half open. The verse is about all of them in spirit: {idea}people deserve a moment to be ready for you.{/idea} A knock and a salaam is a small kindness.
old: We are family, so I can just walk in.
new: Asking first is a way of honoring the people inside, even the closest ones.
try: Knock and say salaam before entering one room at home today, even if the door is open.

title: If they say go back, go back. It is purer.
subtitle: Hearing no without taking offense
then: Ibn Kathir reports that Abu Musa asked permission three times at Umar's door and, with no answer, {idea}simply left.{/idea} He cited the Prophet's ﷺ words that if permission is not given after three times, one should go away. Umar later asked for a witness, and the youngest of the Ansar confirmed it.
now: You show up at a friend's place unannounced. They say through the intercom, "Now is not a good time." Your face gets hot. This verse cools it: {reward}going back is purer for you.{/reward} Their no is not an attack. It is their right, and accepting it is your good deed.
old: If they turn me away, they must not care about me.
new: Turning back gracefully when told no is purer, and Allah sees it.
try: The next time someone says not now, reply with a warm okay and no follow-up guilt.

title: Allah knows what you show and what you hide.
subtitle: Ease in public spaces, with the heart still watched
then: After the manners of entering homes, Allah eases things for places where no one lives and people have a need. The verse closes by reminding them that {idea}Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal.{/idea}
now: The shared office kitchen. The station waiting room. The empty hall at the mosque. No permission needed. But you still know why you walked in. {idea}The ease is real, and so is the One who sees your reason.{/idea}
old: If no one owns the space, nothing I do there matters.
new: Open spaces are an ease from Allah, and my hidden intentions still count.
try: In a shared space today, leave it a little better than you found it.

title: Guarding the eyes is how you guard the heart.
subtitle: The first glance, and what to do with the second
then: Ibn Kathir explains that since looking provokes the heart, the verse joins guarding the gaze with guarding chastity. Jarir asked the Prophet ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he told him {idea}to turn his eyes away.{/idea} An early saying adds that whoever guards his gaze, {reward}Allah illuminates his heart.{/reward}
now: Your feed autoplays something you did not choose. A billboard on the commute. A colleague's photos. The first glance just happens. {idea}The second is a choice.{/idea} Scroll past, look up, look away. Each time is a small gift to your own heart.
new: What I let my eyes rest on shapes my heart, so guarding them is purity.
try: Today, every time your eyes land on something you would not want in your heart, look away within a second.

title: Turn to Allah, all of you, that you may succeed.
subtitle: Modesty for believing women, and a call to everyone

picture.label: What the verse asks of believing women

key.label: How the first women heard it

then: Ibn Kathir notes this distinguished the believing women from the customs of the Jahiliyyah. Aishah said, {reward}may Allah have mercy on the women of the early emigrants:{/reward} when this verse came, they tore their wraps to cover themselves. The verse ends by turning to everyone: {idea}repent to Allah, all of you.{/idea}
now: Everyone has a part of their faith they keep meaning to get to. A habit, a choice of clothes, a way of speaking, a screen they should close. The early emigrant women responded the same day. And the verse does not end with one group. {idea}It ends with all of you, turning back together.{/idea}
old: This verse is about other people's choices.
new: Every believer is called to turn back to Allah, and success lies in that turning.
try: Pick one thing you have been meaning to change for Allah's sake. Take the first step today.
